title: Glimpses of India
book: NCERT First Flight: Textbook in English for Class X
subject: english_literature
author: Lucio Rodrigues; Lokesh Abrol; Arup Kumar Datta
syllabus_note: CBSE 2025-26 English Language and Literature (184): First Flight prose, Chapter 5 (A Baker from Goa; Coorg; Tea from Assam). Assessed through extracts (5 marks), short answers in 40-50 words (3 marks) and long answers in 100-120 words (6 marks).

blocks.title: Bread, coffee and tea
blocks.body:
Wake up to the **jingle** of a baker's bamboo staff in a Goan village. Walk through misty **coffee estates** in Coorg. Ride a train through a 'sea of **tea bushes**' in Assam.

Glimpses of India is three short pieces about three regions of our country: their food, people, history and nature.

blocks.title: The writers
blocks.person: Lucio Rodrigues, Lokesh Abrol, Arup Kumar Datta
blocks.body: **Lucio Rodrigues** writes with nostalgia about the traditions of Goa. **Lokesh Abrol** describes Coorg (Kodagu) like a travel writer. **Arup Kumar Datta**, a writer from Assam known for children's adventure books, tells the story of tea through two schoolboys.
blocks.future: Travel writing, tourism, food history and journalism all begin with close observation of places and people.

blocks.question: Why do the elders in Goa still miss the Portuguese loaves and the old baker?
options: They are part of happy childhood memories and Goan culture
They dislike modern bakeries for no reason
blocks.explanation: Food often carries memories of home and tradition.

blocks.title: The pader and his bread
blocks.body:
**Old memories:** elders in Goa often recall the good old **Portuguese days**, the Portuguese and their famous **loaves of bread**. Though the Portuguese have left, the bakers, the **mixers, moulders** and **furnaces** remain; the age-old, time-tested furnaces still exist and 'the fire in the furnaces has not yet been extinguished'. In some places the sons still carry on the family profession. The bakers are known as **paders**.

**The baker's arrival:** in the narrator's childhood, the baker came at least twice a day: in the morning on his selling round, and again when he returned after emptying his basket. The **jingling thud of his bamboo staff** woke them. He greeted the house with 'Good morning!' and the children ran to him. The servant took the loaves; the children, without brushing their teeth, looked for the **bread-bangles** chosen specially for them. They would not even care to wash their mouths: 'tigers' teeth' would take care of that!

**His dress:** the baker wore a **kabai**, a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees. In the narrator's childhood he wore a shirt and **trousers** shorter than full-length and longer than half pants. Even today, anyone wearing a half pant that reaches just below the knees is told he is dressed **like a pader**!

**Bread in Goan life:** marriage gifts are meaningless without the sweet bread called the **bol**; a party or feast loses its charm without bread; **cakes and bolinhas** are a must for **Christmas**; the lady of the house prepares **sandwiches** for her daughter's engagement.

**A good living:** the baker collected his bills at the end of the month; they were recorded on a wall in **pencil**. Baking was a profitable profession: the baker and his family never starved, and his **plump physique** was an open testimony to this. Even today any person with a jackfruit-like physique is compared to a baker.

blocks.question: What is a 'kabai'?
options: a single-piece long frock reaching down to the knees, worn by the baker
blocks.explanation: It was the baker's dress in the Portuguese days.
option_feedback: The bol and bolinhas are breads.

blocks.question: Which bread is a must at Goan marriages?
blocks.explanation: Marriage gifts are meaningless without the bol.

blocks.title: The land and the people
blocks.body:
**Where:** midway between **Mysore** and the coastal town of **Mangalore**, Coorg or **Kodagu** is the smallest district of **Karnataka**. It is a land of rolling hills, **evergreen rainforests**, spices and **coffee plantations**. Rainforests cover 30% of the district. The writer calls it 'a piece of heaven that must have drifted from the kingdom of god'.

**Weather:** the monsoon pours enough to keep many visitors away; the season of joy begins in **September** and continues till **March**, when the weather is perfect, with some showers thrown in. The air breathes of invigorating coffee.

**The people:** the fiercely independent people of Coorg, the **Kodavus**, are possibly of **Greek or Arabic descent**. One story says part of **Alexander's army** moved south along the coast and settled here. Another theory traces Arab origin: the **kuppia**, a long black coat with an embroidered waist-belt worn by Kodavu men, resembles the **kuffia** worn by Arabs and Kurds. Coorgi homes have a tradition of **hospitality**, and they love to tell tales of **valour**.

**Martial pride:** the **Coorg Regiment** is one of the most decorated in the Indian Army, and the first Chief of the Indian Army, **General Cariappa**, was a Coorgi. The Kodavus are the only people in India permitted to **carry firearms without a licence**.

**River and wildlife:** the river **Kaveri** obtains its water from the hills and forests of Coorg. **Mahaseer**, a large freshwater fish, abound in its waters. Kingfishers dive for their catch, squirrels and langurs drop fruit for the mischief of it, and elephants enjoy being bathed in the river. The wildlife includes Malabar squirrels, langurs and **slender loris**.

**Adventure and places:** river rafting, canoeing, rappelling, rock climbing and mountain biking; climb the **Brahmagiri hills** for a view; walk to the island of **Nisargadhama** across a rope bridge; nearby **Bylakuppe**, India's largest **Tibetan** settlement, with Buddhist monks in red, ochre and yellow robes.

blocks.question: Which people in India may carry firearms without a licence?
Why are the Kodavus thought to be of Arab descent?
options: they came by ship from Arabia in 1947
their kuppia resembles the kuffia worn by Arabs and Kurds
blocks.explanation: Another theory links them to Alexander's army.
option_feedback: The theory is ancient, based on the dress.

blocks.title: Two friends and the story of tea
blocks.body:
**The journey:** **Pranjol**, a youngster from Assam, and his classmate **Rajvir** are going to Assam for the summer vacation. Pranjol's father is the **manager of a tea garden**. At a station, a vendor calls 'Chai-garam... garam-chai'; the boys buy two cups. Rajvir says **over eighty crore cups** of tea are drunk every day throughout the world.

**The landscape:** from the train, Rajvir gazes at a **'sea of tea bushes'**, densely wooded hills, and tall shade-trees. Pranjol, who has grown up on a plantation, is not impressed. Rajvir says Assam has the **largest concentration of plantations in the world**.

**Legends of tea:**
- **Chinese legend:** a Chinese emperor always boiled water before drinking it. One day a few leaves of the twigs burning under the pot fell into the water, giving it a delicious flavour. They were **tea leaves**.
- **Indian legend:** **Bodhidharma**, an ancient Buddhist ascetic, **cut off his eyelids** because he felt sleepy during meditations. **Ten tea plants** grew out of the eyelids; the leaves, put in hot water and drunk, banished sleep.

**History:** tea was first drunk in **China** as far back as **2700 B.C.** Words such as *tea*, *chai* and *chini* come from Chinese. Tea came to **Europe** only in the **sixteenth century** and was drunk more as **medicine** than as a beverage.

**The tea garden:** they reach **Mariani junction**, where Pranjol's parents meet them, and drive to **Dhekiabari Tea Estate**. Women with **bamboo baskets** on their backs, in plastic aprons, are plucking the newly sprouted leaves. It is the **second-flush** or sprouting period, from **May to July**, which yields the **best tea**. Mr Barua is impressed that Rajvir has 'done his homework'.

blocks.title: The three pieces side by side
blocks.body:
| | A Baker from Goa | Coorg | Tea from Assam |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Writer** | Lucio Rodrigues | Lokesh Abrol | Arup Kumar Datta |
| **Region** | Goa, west coast | Kodagu, Karnataka | Assam, north-east |
| **Focus** | the traditional baker (pader) and Portuguese bread | land, people, wildlife and adventure | tea plantations and legends of tea |
| **Key details** | jingle of the bamboo staff; kabai; bol; bolinhas; bills on the wall | Kodavus; Coorg Regiment; General Cariappa; Kaveri; mahaseer; Bylakuppe | Pranjol and Rajvir; Dhekiabari; Chinese and Indian legends; second flush |
| **Mood** | nostalgic and warm | admiring, like a travel guide | curious and informative |

blocks.question: According to the Indian legend, how did tea plants first grow?
options: from a gift by a king
from the eyelids Bodhidharma cut off
from leaves that fell into boiling water
blocks.explanation: Ten tea plants grew from his eyelids.
option_feedback: Tea came to Europe much later.

blocks.question: Which period yields the best tea?
options: the second flush, from May to July
option_feedback: The second flush is May to July.
May to July, the second flush.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Goa words: pader (baker), kabai (dress), bol (marriage), bolinhas (Christmas), bills in pencil on the wall.**
- **Coorg: Kodagu; smallest district of Karnataka; Kodavus; kuppia; Cariappa; Kaveri; mahaseer; Brahmagiri; Nisargadhama; Bylakuppe.**
- **Tea: 2700 B.C. China; 16th century Europe (medicine); 80 crore cups a day; Dhekiabari; second flush May to July.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Saying bolinhas are for marriages: **bol** is for marriages; **bolinhas** for Christmas.
2. Saying Coorg is in Kerala: it is in **Karnataka**, between Mysore and Mangalore.
3. Mixing up the legends: leaves in boiling water = **Chinese** legend; eyelids = **Indian** legend (Bodhidharma).
4. Calling Pranjol the curious one: **Rajvir** read about tea; Pranjol grew up there.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Make three groups: Goa, Coorg and Assam. Each designs a one-page travel poster using five facts from the text. Display and compare.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Which food or drink in your home carries a family memory or tradition? Write three sentences about it, like the narrator of A Baker from Goa.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Geography (Agriculture):** coffee and tea are plantation crops; Assam and Karnataka are leading producers.
- **History:** the Portuguese in Goa until 1961.
- **Analytical paragraph:** use tea production data to practise writing about charts.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
Which of the three places would you most like to visit, and why? Answer in about 120 words using details from the text.

**Model answer:** I would most like to visit Coorg. Lying between Mysore and Mangalore, this smallest district of Karnataka is full of rolling hills, evergreen rainforests and coffee estates, so the air itself smells of coffee. I would go between September and March, when the weather is perfect. I could try river rafting and rock climbing, climb the Brahmagiri hills, and cross the rope bridge to Nisargadhama. I would love to see elephants being bathed in the Kaveri and kingfishers diving for fish, and to visit the Tibetan settlement at Bylakuppe. Above all, I would like to meet the brave and hospitable Kodavus, whose regiment is among the most decorated in the Indian Army.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- A Baker from Goa: the narrator remembers the pader with his jingling bamboo staff, kabai and loaves; bread is part of every Goan celebration; baking was profitable.
- Coorg: a beautiful, misty land of coffee and forests, home to the martial, hospitable Kodavus, the Kaveri, wildlife and adventure sports.
- Tea from Assam: Rajvir and Pranjol travel to a tea estate; Rajvir shares the Chinese and Indian legends and the history of tea.

blocks.title: Exam tips
blocks.body:
- Always say which of the three parts you are answering from.
- Use the local words (pader, kabai, bol, Kodavus, kuppia, second flush); they show close reading.
- 'What do you learn about...?' questions need at least two specific facts from the text.

blocks.front: What were bakers called in Goa?
Name two reasons the Kodavus are thought to have foreign origins.
blocks.back: A story says part of Alexander's army settled there (Greek); their kuppia resembles the Arab kuffia.

blocks.front: What is the Chinese legend about tea?
blocks.back: Leaves from burning twigs fell into an emperor's boiling water and gave it a delicious flavour.

blocks.front: Which period gives the best tea?
blocks.back: The second flush, from May to July.
